detail.title: Utilizing Foreign Currency-Denominated Collaterals for Naira Loans and the Position of the Central Bank of Nigeria
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the evolving regulatory stance of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) concerning Naira-denominated loans secured by foreign currency (FCY) collateral. While the Foreign Exchange Manual 2018 previously permitted this practice under strict conditions, mandating use in approved sectors and restricting collateral instruments, widespread non-compliance introduced significant systemic risk.

In response, the CBN issued a restrictive directive on April 8, 2024, which now prohibits the use of FCY collateral for Naira loans, with the only exceptions being Eurobonds issued by the Federal Government of Nigeria and guarantees from foreign banks.

This pivotal regulatory shift addresses CBN's core concerns: currency mismatch, increased financial instability for lenders, and the speculative hoarding of foreign exchange, which depletes market liquidity. 

The paper details the resultant implications, particularly for Nigerian banks, which face a 150% risk-weighting penalty on all non-compliant exposures, underscoring the CBN's strategic preference for channeling foreign currency into the market over its use as static collateral.

title: DO STATE-OWNED BANKS REDUCE THEIR DIVIDENDS DURING AN ECONOMIC CRISIS? THE SWISS CASE
affiliations: University of Fribourg - University of Fribourg - Faculty of Economics and Social Science, University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne) and University of Lausanne, HEC-Lausanne

detail.title: DO STATE-OWNED BANKS REDUCE THEIR DIVIDENDS DURING AN ECONOMIC CRISIS? THE SWISS CASE
detail.abstract: Several financial authorities, including the IMF and ECB, recommended that banks limit dividend payments during the economic crisis caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. This study examines how Swiss state-owned banks responded to these recommendations. Using a difference-in-differences analysis of panel data from 2014 to 2021, we find that, compared to other Swiss banks, Swiss state-owned banks increased their dividend payouts during the crisis. Furthermore, we show that these higher payouts are not the result of increased profitability or liquidity. However, a reduction in lending activity among state-owned banks appears to have contributed to excess liquidity, which may have been distributed as dividends. Finally, we find no significant differences in dividend payouts between public and private state-owned banks, suggesting that financial market pressure does not affect our results. Overall, this study advances our understanding of the role of state ownership in banking, which remains important in many countries, especially during an economic crisis.

title: Riding the Silver Tsunami in Pursuit of Economic Democracy: Economic Inequality, Baby Boomers, and Worker Cooperatives

detail.title: Riding the Silver Tsunami in Pursuit of Economic Democracy: Economic Inequality, Baby Boomers, and Worker Cooperatives
detail.abstract: The "American Dream," a national ethos centered on the belief in equal opportunity and upward socioeconomic mobility through hard work, has evolved significantly over time. Originally, it embodied ideals of liberty, justice, and economic democracy, opposing excessive wealth accumulation and economic inequality. However, over the 20th century, it became synonymous with individual economic success, particularly represented by Baby Boomers who thrived in the post-World War II economic boom. Today, Americans face an increasingly wide income and wealth gap that echoes the conditions of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, raising questions about the Dream's accessibility and relevance. This Article explores how worker cooperatives, which emphasize shared prosperity and democratic ownership, offer a pathway to reinvigorate the American Dream in the 21st century. By converting aging businesses owned by Baby Boomers into worker cooperatives, we can move toward an inclusive economic model that fosters social mobility, equitable opportunity, and sustainable prosperity. This Article examines the history, current conditions, and potential of worker cooperatives as a transformative business model for America 's economic future.

title: Designing an Accessible Classroom: Beyond the Physical Spaces

detail.title: Designing an Accessible Classroom: Beyond the Physical Spaces
detail.abstract: The discourse of accessibility in higher education has long been dominated by attention to physical environments: ramps, elevators, and adaptive furniture. While these infrastructural elements are necessary, they are insufficient for fostering inclusive participation. This article argues that accessibility must be theorized and enacted as a multidimensional construct encompassing pedagogical design, digital affordances, and socio-emotional conditions of learning. Drawing on Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and scholarship from disability studies, inclusive pedagogy, and digital accessibility, I examine how accessibility functions not as a checklist of accommodations but as a relational practice embedded in teaching, technology, and classroom culture. The article concludes with recommendations for shifting institutional and pedagogical orientations from reactive compliance to anticipatory equity.

title: The Epistemology of Construction Management: From Production to Cognition

detail.title: The Epistemology of Construction Management: From Production to Cognition
detail.abstract: Construction Management (CM) has long existed as a practice-but only recently has it emerged as a self-conscious field of inquiry. Historically, its knowledge base was borrowed f engineering, architecture, and project management rather than developed from within. Over the past three decades, however, original theoretical frameworks-such as Transformation-Flow-Value (TFV) theory, Temporary Multi-Organization (TMO) theory, Construction Complexity theory, and Socio-Technical Systems perspective-have begun to articulate how construction knowledge is generated, validated, and shared. This paper traces the epistemological evolution of Construction Management, arguing that the discipline is shifting from a productioncentered to a cognition-centered paradigm of knowing. Construction is repositioned not merely as a technical process but as a form of situated, reflective intelligence-a collective act of knowing through making. The paper introduces Quantum PDSA, grounded in the Confucian principle of 慎独 (Shèn Dú), which frames reflective learning as both an ethical and cognitive act within professional practice. It concludes that the future epistemology of CM must integrate systems thinking, sustainability, and cognitive awareness to navigate the complexity of a digitized, post-industrial built environment.

title: Knowledge Management Systems and the Sustainability of Small Businesses in Emerging Economies, Amidst Crisis

detail.title: Knowledge Management Systems and the Sustainability of Small Businesses in Emerging Economies, Amidst Crisis
detail.abstract: Small businesses form the backbone of most emerging economies, accounting for a substantial share of employment, poverty alleviation, and economic resilience. Yet, they remain highly vulnerable to crises such as economic shocks, health pandemics, and policy instability. This paper explores the role of Knowledge Management Systems (KMS) in enhancing the sustainability of small businesses in emerging economies, with a particular focus on resource-constrained environments. Building on the knowledge-based theory of the firm, the study highlights the critical role of knowledge capture, storage, transfer, and use in strengthening resilience and continuity. It proposes a four-pillar framework documentation, technology enablement, people and culture, and ecosystem support to guide the design and adoption of KMS for small enterprises. The paper argues that embedding KMS into small business strategy is not only a managerial choice but a development imperative, with implications for entrepreneurs, policymakers, and development partners.

detail.abstract: While the Montgomery Bus Boycott is widely celebrated, its economic impact on Montgomery has been understudied. This paper reexamines the Montgomery Bus Boycott with two goals: 1. Determining if the Montgomery Bus Boycott affected the city’s public finances. 2. Forecasting the probability that city revenues would have fallen below expenditure. Our analysis demonstrates that the Boycott had a negative effect on the city’s public finances, particularly in the area of policing and fire services, driven by the city's “get tough” policy response to the boycott. Using historical financial records and time-series forecasting (ARIMA), this paper quantifies the growing fiscal strain experienced by the city. Although Montgomery maintained budget surpluses during the Boycott period, projections indicate a rising probability of deficits had the protest continued. These findings highlight the economic leverage wielded by organized civil resistance and puts into focus the material costs municipal governments incurr when confronting social movements.

title: Hybrid Deep Learning Architectures for Value-at-Risk Forecasting: Integrating LSTM and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks

detail.title: Hybrid Deep Learning Architectures for Value-at-Risk Forecasting: Integrating LSTM and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
detail.abstract: This study proposes a novel framework for Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecasting by integrating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with recently developed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) variants, trained directly on a quantile loss objective. We benchmark the proposed models, including an enhanced LSTM-MultKAN variant, against a standard LSTM-Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and a suite of ARMA-GARCH models. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on information criteria, we optimize the specifications of the GARCH benchmarks using a machine-learning-based validation based on the out-of-sample performance as measured by quantile loss, ensuring a fair comparison. Furthermore, to address the interpretability challenge of neural networks, a deep interpretability analysis is conducted, employing SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) alongside the inherent transparency of the KAN architecture. The LSTM-KAN variants show statistically significant improvements in predictive accuracy and robustness, establishing a clear performance advantage over traditional GARCH models. Within the network architectures, the LSTM-MultKAN variant demonstrates the strongest performance, outperforming the standard LSTM-MLP benchmark. Our interpretability analysis reveals that this superior performance is not arbitrary; the network models learn to identify well-documented financial phenomena, such as volatility clustering and the leverage effect. By achieving both accuracy and interpretability, this study presents a powerful and trustworthy VaR forecasting tool for researchers and risk managers.

title: Carbon Accounting and ESG Compliance: An IFRS S1 and S2-Based Assessment of Nigeria’s Cement Industry

detail.title: Carbon Accounting and ESG Compliance: An IFRS S1 and S2-Based Assessment of Nigeria’s Cement Industry
detail.abstract: This research investigates the extent of compliance with IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 sustainability and climate disclosure requirements across Nigeria’s major cement producers—Dangote Cement Plc, BUA Cement Plc, and Lafarge Africa Plc. Using a quantitative content analysis of annual and sustainability reports from 2022 to 2024, the study constructs a disclosure index based on IFRS S1 and S2 guidelines to quantify compliance levels. The results show significant conformity with IFRS S1 (average compliance score of 66.2%) and IFRS S2 (68.3%), reflecting credible and consistent carbon accounting approaches aligned with international frameworks such as the GHG Protocol. Correlation and regression analyses reveal that operational efficiency, gender diversity, and external assurance positively influence disclosure quality, while implementation challenges remain statistically insignificant. The findings confirm that Nigeria’s cement industry has achieved notable progress in integrating sustainability and financial disclosures, underscoring its preparedness for mandatory adoption of IFRS S1 and S2 by 2027. The study contributes empirical evidence for emerging markets transitioning toward investor-grade sustainability reporting standards.

title: Deciphering the Web of Industry 4.0: Digital Transformation in Commercial Banks
affiliations: University of Queensland, Queensland University of Technology, Queensland University of Technology and University of Canberra

detail.title: Deciphering the Web of Industry 4.0: Digital Transformation in Commercial Banks
detail.abstract: The existing body of literature exploring innovations and digital transformations in the banking sector emphasizes the emergence of competitive business models by FinTechs and digital banks. Despite their significance, commercial banks remain the predominant players. Thus, comprehending how commercial banks assimilate disruptive technologies encompassing Industry 4.0's technological advancements is crucial. This systematic literature review aims to pinpoint the primary strategies commercial banks employ in response to heightened competition and crises. Analysing 238 articles up to 2023, we crafted a conceptual framework resembling a 'spider's web.' This framework illuminates how Industry 4.0 initiates a cohesive digitalization flow. Our findings reveal an interdependent relationship among elements in three distinct groups, underscoring that the success of the digital transformation hinges on banks' comprehensive understanding of these relationships and their adoption of a holistic approach.

title: Presidential Infrastructure Expenditures and Socioeconomic Inequality: The 2025 White House Ballroom Project as a Case Study in Fiscal Priorities and Unrest Risks

detail.title: Presidential Infrastructure Expenditures and Socioeconomic Inequality: The 2025 White House Ballroom Project as a Case Study in Fiscal Priorities and Unrest Risks
detail.abstract: This paper examines the implications of the $250 million White House State Ballroom project announced in July 2025, against a backdrop of federal budget cuts to essential social programs and rising generational inequality. The privately funded project-with demolition of the East Wing beginning October 20, 2025-highlights perceived fiscal misalignment during a period of significant austerity measures affecting millions of Americans. Drawing on the 1968 Kerner Report's linkage of poverty to civil unrest, this study analyzes how recent federal budget legislation cutting programs including Medicaid ($863 billion over 10 years), SNAP ($295 billion), and education programs ($330 billion) exacerbates inequality amid stagnating homeownership rates for younger generations. While Gen Z homeownership stands at approximately 26%, this represents a plateau from prior years despite their entering prime homebuying ages. Historical U.S. uprisings and global examples demonstrate unrest risks supported by IMF data indicating that inequality increases correlate with civil disorder. We argue that such expenditures, even when privately funded, could serve as symbolic flashpoints for social instability without policy interventions. Policy recommendations include enhanced transparency measures for privately funded government projects and restoration of funding for essential aid programs.

title: Reflection on the Documentary Plastic Island (2021)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Reflection on the Documentary Plastic Island (2021)
detail.abstract: Here is a reflection on the documentary Plastic Island (2021) Reflection on Plastic Island Watching Plastic Island, I was struck by several major themes and the emotional, ethical, and practical implications of plastic pollution-especially in a setting like Indonesia, where the documentary takes place. The fact that it follows a musician, a biologist and a lawyer working together to fight plastic waste shows how complex the issue is, and how it spans culture, science, law and daily life. Here are key take-aways and my reflections: * Scope and scale of the problem The documentary makes clear that plastic waste isn't just a local nuisance-it's systemic. The title itself ("Plastic Island") evokes the almost-overwhelming mass of plastic debris, the idea of islands of waste, the shifting nature of the pollution. It's easy to ignore plastic because it seems small, but when aggregated the impact is huge. This leads me to reflect: when our individual actions feel small (using a plastic straw, throwing away a bottle) we might think "what difference does it make?" But when we zoom out, the cumulative effect is massive. It challenges me to consider how my habits, and the habits of those around me, feed into a global problem.

title: Private Equity, Public Capital, and Litigation Risk
affiliations: University of Oxford - Said Business School and Texas A&M University School of Law

detail.title: Private Equity, Public Capital, and Litigation Risk
detail.abstract: For nearly a century, securities regulation has drawn a sharp line: firms that seek to raise capital from the public must comply with strict governance and disclosure duties, while firms that remain "private" may organize their internal governance structures as they see fit. But the line between public and private capital is now eroding. Private equity firms, once funded solely by institutions, increasingly raise capital from ordinary investors, while remaining outside the reach of securities regulation through a combination of complex financial structures and well-worn legal exemptions. As a result, asset classes long confined to qualified investors are now being offered to the public, but without the protection traditionally attached to public offerings. This Article argues that this retailization of private equity creates a significant regulatory gap. Practices normalized in institutional settings-misleading performance metrics, manipulable valuations, opaque fees, limited liquidity, and fiduciary duty waivers-become significant litigation risks when ordinary investors enter the picture. Financial regulators are ill-equipped to address these risks, a problem exacerbated by the deregulatory agenda of the last two decades. But while public enforcement is likely to remain ineffective, private equity's retailization opens a new and potentially more powerful avenue for holding firms to account: private enforcement. By broadening their investor base, private equity firms have exposed themselves to litigation under a wide range of domains, from contract to tort, from fraud to consumer protection. These doctrines, long thought peripheral to private equity, are often broader and stricter than traditional securities regulation. This Article charts how private enforcement could reshape the industry and explores how the future of private equity will increasingly be shaped by judges, not regulators.

title: Clarifying Trinko as Precedent in EHR and AI-Memory Duty to Deal Cases: A New Institutional Economics Approach
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Clarifying Trinko as Precedent in EHR and AI-Memory Duty to Deal Cases: A New Institutional Economics Approach
detail.abstract: By clarifying the bases for SCOTUS' opinion in Verizon Communications Inc. v. Law Offices of Curtis V. Trinko, LLP, (2004) ( Trinko),  we hope to reduce two distinct errors. The false positive error is citing Trinko as precedent when it isn't. This error is so prevalent it has earned the nickname of "Trinko Creep." The false negative error is not citing Trinko when it should be. We argue that this error will be growing in the future as Trinko should be precedent in cases involving regulated access rights to sensitive consumer data in electronic health records (EHRs) and and Agentic AI Long Term Memory (AI-LTM).

detail.abstract: This study develops the Islamic Circular Fiscal System (ICFS) as a conceptual model for optimizing Islamic public revenue sources in a sustainable manner. Using a qualitativedescriptive approach based on library research, this study integrates the principles of maqāṣid al-sharīʿah, circular economy theory, and Islamic fiscal policy literature to formulate circular mechanisms in the management of zakat, infaq, and waqf. The results of the study introduce two main frameworks: the Circular Fiscal Governance Framework (CFGF), which functions as a model for institutional governance and coordination between Islamic fiscal institutions, and the Circular Fiscal Performance Index (CFPI), which is proposed as an evaluative instrument for circular fiscal effectiveness. Through the ICFS approach, this study emphasizes the importance of integrating sharia values with economic sustainability principles in forming a productive, fair, and transparent Islamic fiscal system. The study also highlights the role of digital governance, public-private partnerships, and the strengthening of Islamic financial instruments (such as waqf sukuk) as prerequisites for ICFS implementation. Due to its conceptual nature, this study recommends empirical testing of the effectiveness of CFGF and CFPI in the practice of Islamic fiscal policy in the future.

title: A Short Note on a Unified Stable-Law Limit for Adaptive Heavy-Tailed Financial Returns
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Short Note on a Unified Stable-Law Limit for Adaptive Heavy-Tailed Financial Returns
detail.abstract: This short note highlights the core innovation behind a new generalized central limit theorem (GCLT) designed for heavy-tailed, dependent, and online-updated financial returns. The key contribution is a unified asymptotic result showing that a return process simultaneously exhibiting (i) regularly varying innovations, (ii) stochastic-volatility dependence, and (iii) online parameter drift still satisfies an α-stable limit theorem for cumulative returns. A minimal version of the theorem is stated and proved using only regular variation, point-process convergence, and a drift-negligibility argument.

title: Regional Autonomy and Development: Evidence from Madhya Pradesh – Chhattisgarh Split in India
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Regional Autonomy and Development: Evidence from Madhya Pradesh – Chhattisgarh Split in India

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We exploit the creation of Chhattisgarh (CH) from Madhya Pradesh (MP) in 2000 as a natural experiment to study how regional autonomy affects economic development through administrative proximity and political accountability. Using both difference-in-differences and difference-in-discontinuities designs, we compare villages straddling the new state border before and after the split. Villages in CH near the border experienced significantly faster economic growth—measured by nighttime lights, expansion of private firms and non-farm employment, and improved provision of public goods—than comparable MP villages. These gains are not explained by political stability, party ideology, or migration. Instead, they arise from a more responsive local elite in-charge of the new administration as well as closer proximity to the new state capital, Raipur, which enhanced bureaucratic oversight and political accountability. The results demonstrate that the geography of administration—the distance between citizens and state institutions—can shape development outcomes as powerfully as formal political institutions.

title: The Legal Structure of the Patent System in the Context of IA

detail.title: The Legal Structure of the Patent System in the Context of IA
detail.abstract: Chapter 3 of the book "Artificial Intelligence and Patents: foundations, inventorship and the Theory of Entrepreneurship", which derives from the PhD thesis of the author defended at Rio de Janeiro State University. The research seeks to contribute to the theoretical debate surrounding the legal protection of patents on inventions generated by AI, whether autonomous or not. This Chapter 3 focused on researching the other legal issues affecting the patent system as a result of the use of artificial intelligence systems in inventive processes. The impacts on the legal requirements of novelty, inventive step, industrial application, descriptive sufficiency and eligibility were assessed, as well as the great controversy over inventorship and ownership. The topics of civil liability and compulsory licensing were also superficially addressed.

title: Economic Recovery in High vs. Low-Priced Housing Areas After Disaster: Paradise, California's 2018 Camp Fire
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title: Economic Recovery in High vs. Low-Priced Housing Areas After Disaster: Paradise, California's 2018 Camp Fire
detail.abstract: This study examines the uneven recovery trajectories of high and low priced housing areas following the 2018 Camp Fire in Paradise, California, one of the deadliest wildfires in U.S. history. Using descriptive data from the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI), the American Community Survey (ACS), local building permit data, and Butte County assessor reports, this paper investigates how socioeconomic conditions shaped post disaster housing and fiscal recovery. Results show that high value residential areas recovered substantially faster than low value neighborhoods, driven by greater insurance coverage, higher resource capacity, and early reinvestment incentives. In contrast, low income residents faced slower rebuilding rates, prolonged displacement, and permanent relocation, amplifying wealth inequality. The findings reinforce the concept of disaster gentrification, where reconstruction processes disproportionately benefit affluent households and reshape community composition. Policy recommendations include expanding affordable housing subsidies, supporting modular rebuilding, and establishing community land trusts to ensure social equity during post disaster recovery. The Paradise case illustrates that true resilience requires integrating equity into disaster recovery planning.

title: Between Platforms and Protection: Social Security Gaps and Inclusive Prosperity for Indonesian Ride-Hailing Drivers
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Between Platforms and Protection: Social Security Gaps and Inclusive Prosperity for Indonesian Ride-Hailing Drivers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study relies exclusively on secondary analysis of publicly available data and reports. No primary data collection involving human participants was conducted by the author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
In Indonesia, The World Bank Gini Inequality Index (2025) suggest progress in reducing inequality (39% to 35%, 2014-2024). The National Statistics Bureau (BPS) (2025) reports the lowest level of unemployment since post-pandemic era as per February 2025 at 4.76%. However, recent four-day nationwide protests in August-September 2025 triggered by the increase in compensation of lawmakers (later rescinded) marked a perception of increasing inequality on the ground. A 2024 Kantar report estimated that 59% of the Indonesian workforce is informal, of which 50% are gig workers. The majority representation of informal workers, and the significant representation of gig workers therein, suggests that gig workers are a key driver of Indonesian economy. While formally working on digital platforms, their position as informal workers limits access to mandatory employment benefits. 

This study evaluates this paradox between prosperity and perceived inequality using the three pillars of inclusive prosperity framework (Acemoglu & Robinson, 2013; Acemoglu, 2019) based on existing quantitative survey data collected from Indonesian motorbike gig workers (Brailovskaya et al. 2024a, 2024b; N=3,502 active, inactive, and offline drivers). For the first pillar, Economic Growth and Improved Living Standards, I compare incomes between active and offline drivers to assess whether platform work improves livelihoods or exposes hidden vulnerabilities. For the second pillar, Economic Opportunities and Good Jobs, I examine drivers' exit opportunities and motivations, including for inactive drivers, to evaluate whether gig work translates into economic opportunities or locks workers into informality without protection. For the third pillar, Institutions and Technology to Enable Opportunities, I quantify barriers in social protection participation rate, formal union participation, and gender equality, revealing the institutional shortcomings that limit access to protection. 

Findings highlight the gap between the ideal narrative of digital platforms as opportunity providers and the reality of limited social protection, offering implications for more inclusive policy design.

detail.abstract: Since the onset of the U.S.-China trade dispute, economic tensions between the two countries have persisted, with the Biden administration maintaining a hardline stance on China. With the recent return of the Trump administration, a large-scale tariff war is once again anticipated, making thorough analysis and policy responses increasingly critical. title: Axioms for Predictability: Toward a Turing-Style Epistemology on Cantor Space
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Axioms for Predictability: Toward a Turing-Style Epistemology on Cantor Space
detail.abstract: We formalize a minimal, modular axiom system under which meaningful predictability guarantees are provable for sequential observations. Worlds are infinite sequences on a finite alphabet (Cantor space). Observers choose forecasts from finite histories. We isolate continuity, compactness, dominance, capacity, and temporal regularity as orthogonal structural assumptions. Removing any one of these sabotages at least one key predictive guarantee (calibration, posterior merging, no-regret, identification in the limit). We state Turing-style results: impossibility via diagonalization and undecidability, optimality in the uncomputable limit (Solomonoff), and positive consistency theorems under our axioms. Proofs are developed in full detail, with complete bibliography.

title: Taxing the New Oil: A Feasibility Analysis of an Excise Tax on Computational Resources

detail.title: Taxing the New Oil: A Feasibility Analysis of an Excise Tax on Computational Resources
detail.abstract: This article argues that the rise of AI has outpaced legacy tax architectures and proposes a new Pigouvian-style excise tax on the tangible inputs of AI—computational resources—to capture value, curb negative externalities, and fund the social transition it accelerates. The paper develops and compares three bases for such a tax: (A) electricity consumed by data centers (administratively simple but blunt), (B) a one-time levy on accelerator hardware (clear incidence but misaligned with lifetime usage), and (C) a hybrid performance-linked model that tiers specific rates by hardware characteristics such as Thermal Design Power (TDP), which better aligns incentives toward energy-efficient compute and is paired with a fit-for-purpose Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) regime that avoids the shortcomings of Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE). Recognizing extreme capital mobility and subsidy competition in data-center siting, the paper contends that unilateral action would trigger investment flight; therefore, feasibility hinges on multilateral coordination—ideally via an OECD/G20-style framework establishing common technical standards, minimum rates, and cooperation mechanisms. An indicative revenue analysis suggests substantial yields even at modest rates, with proceeds earmarked to an AI Transition Fund for social safety nets, large-scale reskilling, and potentially a universal dividend. The article concludes with a three-phase roadmap—technical standardization, multilateral agreement, and coordinated implementation—positioning a compute excise as a pragmatic, innovation-directing tool to make the AI economy more sustainable and equitable.

title: Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence and Environmental Sustainability
affiliations: IZA Institute of Labor Economics, University of Ottawa - Department of Economics, Wilfrid Laurier University - School of Business & Economics and University of Ottawa

detail.title: Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence and Environmental Sustainability

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly viewed as both a potential driver of environmental sustainability and a contributor to global energy demand. Yet little is known about how the public interprets these dual narratives. We conducted a pre-registered online experiment (N = 2142) on a representative sample of the United States to examine how framing the environmental impacts of AIas positive or negativeaffects beliefs, policy preferences, and behavioral intentions. Positive messaging led to greater optimism about AIs environmental impact, lower support for regulation, increased support for government subsidies of AI-enabled technology adoption, and increased consumer preferences for AI-enabled appliances. Negative messaging increased support for regulation and decreased support for government subsidies. Consistent with previous evidence, the messenger (scientist vs journalist) had minimal impact. Our findings highlight the power of environmental framing in shaping public narratives around AI, with implications for science communication, sustainability governance, and technology acceptance.

title: The Devil Is in the Details: State-Mandated Personal Finance Education and Financial Well-Being
affiliations: Follette School of Public Affairs and Montana State University - Bozeman - Department of Agricultural Economics and Economics

detail.title: The Devil Is in the Details: State-Mandated Personal Finance Education and Financial Well-Being

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Research documents the positive effects of state-required financial education in high school on downstream financial outcomes but pools different types of mandates. Do state policies embedding personal finance content into another course have the same effect as those that require a standalone course? This paper considers the relative effects of the two policy levers on credit scores and subjective financial well-being, using data from states implementing these policies in similar years. Our results show that states requiring a full semester of coursework improve both credit scores and subjective measures of financial well-being, while states allowing more flexibility in implementing personal finance coursework into other classes do not.

title: Stablecoins, Tokens, and Global Financial Dominance: Data Integrity and Systemic Stability
affiliations: Regional Advisory Commision on Financial Markets

detail.title: Stablecoins, Tokens, and Global Financial Dominance: Data Integrity and Systemic Stability

keywords: Global Financial Dominance: Data Integrity and Systemic Stability

detail.abstract: Today's interconnected global economy is underpinned by three of the most essential attributes of economic development: trust, confidence, and stability. Accurate and timely dissemination of underlying data across all tiers of the economy is paramount for achieving these attributes. In light of improving technology platforms-e.g. Artificial Intelligence, Big Data Analytics and Distributed Ledger Technology-the quality, provenance, and integrity of data have become high-risk yet high-return economic propositions. The economic stakes are huge within the domain of financial services through potential profound changes to market structures, economic models, and operating paradigms. Data integrity within the financial ecosystem is a cross-cutting theme linking technology, functionality, monetary flow, and national policy concerns. Various digital currencies, stablecoins, economic innovation, Digital Financial Assets (DFAs), and other financial instruments are subject to an intricate interplay between trust, confidence, and systemic stability [1]. The topic of focus pertains to emerging stablecoins, tokens, and Digital Financial Assets (DFAs) as systemic potential instruments for "Global Financial Dominance". Existing major fiat currencies and their stablecoin equivalents, China's Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), and various national currencies under aligned Digital Financial Assets (DFAs) dominate the International Monetary System (IMS) [2]. Priorities surrounding data integrity assurance are fundamental in addressing systemic risks that constrain the fulfilment of institutional market trust and confidence, which are vital to national secure.

title: Direct Democracy and Political Extremism
affiliations: University of Basel and University of Basel

detail.title: Direct Democracy and Political Extremism

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how citizens right to directly decide on policies through popular initiatives affects the attractiveness of extreme candidates in representative elections. In our theoretical framework, single prominent policy issues on which individual voters hold extreme views get a large weight in their assessment of candidates, thereby favoring ideologically extreme ones. If citizens can decide the controversial policy issues separately on the ballot, this decouples the issues from legislative politics and moderate candidates become relatively more attractive to voters. We apply our theory to U.S. state legislative elections and find that ideologically extreme candidates receive significantly lower voter support in initiative than in non-initiative states. This holds in particular for states with low qualification requirements for initiatives. In concurrent elections for the U.S. House we do not observe this difference in the electoral success of extreme candidates between initiative and non-initiative states. The effect seems partly mediated by lower campaign donations to extreme candidates.

title: Sick or Unemployed? Examining Transitions into Sickness Insurance at Unemployment Benefit Exhaustion
affiliations: CPB Netherlands Bureau of Economic Policy Analysis and Lancaster University

detail.title: Sick or Unemployed? Examining Transitions into Sickness Insurance at Unemployment Benefit Exhaustion

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Spikes in exits at unemployment insurance (UI) benefit exhaustion into other benefit schemes such as sickness insurance (SI) are well-documented. These spikes could be driven by relatively healthy workers maximizing their total duration of benefit receipt, or workers in ill health who remain on UI while incapable of working. While the first explanation calls for a stricter SI and UI system, the second highlights the need for increased information provision. We study the importance of these explanations by first documenting a spike in exits into SI at UI benefit exhaustion in the Netherlands. Comparing detailed health and labor market characteristics of exit cohorts, we show that the spike is unlikely to be driven by maximizing behavior of relatively healthy workers. Instead, our results point to catch-up of initial non-take-up of SI by workers with substantial mental and physical health conditions. This opposes earlier work on substitution between UI and SI/DI.

title: Housing Market Responses to Constrained Mobility Rights – Evidence from A School Enrollment Reform for Migrant Children
affiliations: Syracuse University,  and Shandong University

detail.title: Housing Market Responses to Constrained Mobility Rights – Evidence from A School Enrollment Reform for Migrant Children

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Mobility matches open housing markets. With constrained mobility and partially open housing markets, market responses reflect the constraints. We study this mechanism by examining disparity in access to public schools across socio-economic groups, focusing on properties near primary schools accessible to migrant students under social integration policies in a Chinese megacity. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we uncover complex spatial and market dynamics: while house prices close to ordinary primary schools remained relatively stable, house prices farther away declined markedly. This differential impact suggests the interaction between a potential "peer effect" and an "amenity effect." The rental rates showed little change from the migrant inflow and native flights. The reform also triggered a decrease in second-hand house sales, coupled with increased rental activities. This study highlights the effect of school enrollment policies on urban spatial dynamics, with significant implications for policymakers seeking to promote social integration in megacities.

title: Sick Pay Policies and the Socioeconomic Gradient in Health and Welfare
affiliations: University of Fribourg - Faculty of Economics and Social Science, University of Göttingen - Faculty of Economic Sciences and University of Göttingen - School of Law, Economics, Social Sciences

detail.title: Sick Pay Policies and the Socioeconomic Gradient in Health and Welfare

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Sick pay compensates for income loss during illness. However, it may distort labor supply by affecting gross wages if paid by employers and net wages if financed by social insurance contributions. We develop a dynamic general equilibrium model with endogenous, biologically founded health and aging in an education-stratified society to study how the level and financing of sick pay affect the socioeconomic health gradient, income inequality, life expectancy, and welfare. Our analysis shows that reducing the sick pay replacement rate would significantly raise distributional disparities in income and health in Germany. We also show that the individually preferred sick pay replacement rate decreases with the level of educational attainment and that most individuals prefer employer-funded sick pay over public financing.

title: The Causal Effects of Trump's Reelection on Business Expectations of German Firms
affiliations: Friedrich Alexander University Erlangen Nuremberg and Ifo Institute

detail.title: The Causal Effects of Trump's Reelection on Business Expectations of German Firms

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies the causal effects of the 2024 US presidential election on business expectations of German manufacturing firms. It exploits the variation in the timing of survey responses to identify shifts in expectations around the election. The probability of reporting negative expectations increases by 12 percentage points. The effect is driven by exporters, especially those exposed to the US economy. It is concentrated among firms that had not anticipated Trump’s re-election, indicating rational expectation updating. Firms reduce planned investment expenditures. The results provide novel evidence that firms are attentive and quickly revise expectations in response to salient policy events.

title: The Evolution of Hours Worked and the Gender Wage Gap: Theory and Evidence from Four Countries
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Milano - Dipartimento di Economia Politica e Aziendale (DEPA), Georgia State University and CNRS

detail.title: The Evolution of Hours Worked and the Gender Wage Gap: Theory and Evidence from Four Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We consider the contribution of the intensive margin of labor supply (hours worked above zero) to the gender wage gap across four economies (Germany, France, US, UK) over a long time-horizon. We first build a model in which firms offer two wage contracts  one that pays a fixed wage but allows workers to choose their preferred number of hours up to full time, and a second in which wages are relative to imperfectly observable productivity but hours can be limitless. The former includes part- and full-time work, while the latter represents a class of workers who often must supply very long hours but who can then earn potentially unlimited remuneration. We then apply a Oaxaca decomposition for part-, full-, and over-time workers to observe the relative contribution of sorting and remuneration across these hours regimes over time and across countries. Through this, we show that while female employment in over-time work increased and the gender wage decreased, this was not driven by increasing selection but rather by a decrease in the unexplained portion of the wage gap over time. We conclude by considering the contribution of unions and labor market flexibility to these cross-country differences.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Poverty Graphical Coding Map (PGC-Map), a new multidimensional index designed to measure and analyse poverty beyond traditional income-based definitions. Grounded in a capability and opportunity framework, PGC-Map seeks to capture the multifaceted nature of poverty by integrating four essential dimensions: Capabilities, Opportunities, basic living Conditions, and protection from Exclusion. Each dimension is measured using a set of quantitative indicators normalized on a 0-100 deprivation scale, allowing for crosscountry comparability and longitudinal tracking. PGC-Map not only reflects the current state of poverty but also exposes structural barriers that perpetuate deprivation. The index incorporates a regenerative mathematical formulation that penalizes severe multidimensional deprivation and optionally adjusts for inequality within populations. By merging theoretical robustness with policy applicability, PGC-Map aims to serve as a decisionsupport tool for governments, international organizations, and researchers. It expands the analytical capacity of poverty studies and provides a new lens through which to design, evaluate, and target poverty reduction policies in an era where economic, social, and digital inequalities are increasingly intertwined.

title: Reconceptualizing the Role of Women Lawyers in Climate Justice
affiliations: University of Nairobi - School of Law, Chartered Institute of Arbitrators ( Kenya)

detail.title: Reconceptualizing the Role of Women Lawyers in Climate Justice
detail.abstract: The idea of climate justice seeks to foster the rights of people and communities that are most vulnerable to climate impacts including people living in small island nations and those in developing countries. Effective climate action requires climate justice to be realized. It envisages the participation of people and communities most impacted by climate change including those in developing countries, indigenous communities, women and children as part of the climate solution in order to foster climate justice. This paper critically explores the role of women lawyers in climate justice. The paper argues that women lawyers have a crucial role to play in fostering climate justice. It discusses the concept of climate justice and highlights its core tenets. It further highlights ways through which women lawyers contribute in achieving the ideal of climate justice. The paper further examines the progress made towards embracing the role of women lawyers in climate justice and challenges thereof. It also offers some ideas towards strengthening the role of women lawyers in climate justice.

The analysis explores the role of effective climate policy, stressing the relevance of coordinated approaches that match instruments to technology maturity and local context.

title: Reforming Investor State Arbitration: Treaty Options and Practical Steps for Pakistan

detail.title: Reforming Investor State Arbitration: Treaty Options and Practical Steps for Pakistan
detail.abstract: Investor–state arbitration has evolved from a niche legal mechanism into the central system for resolving disputes between investors and sovereign States. However, growing criticism over legitimacy, cost, and asymmetry has triggered reform efforts across the ICSID and UNCITRAL frameworks. This article situates Pakistan’s experience within the global reform debate, examining landmark disputes such as Reko Diq and energy-sector claims to illustrate structural weaknesses in traditional bilateral investment treaties. It proposes substantive and procedural reforms to restore balance between investor protection and regulatory sovereignty.

detail.abstract: Despite unprecedented access to financial information, young adults remain financially illiterate. This paper examines the evolving role of financial literacy education in higher education and society, proposing a hybrid model that combines structured academic instruction, digital tools, and intergenerational dialogue. Drawing on research from Yale, Stanford, and Lusardi & Mitchell (2014), and informed by my personal experience as an international student turned finance professional, this paper revisits my earlier position that universities should make personal finance mandatory. I now argue that while financial literacy must be treated as a core life skill, the delivery model must evolve to match the realities of the digital and AI age. Financial knowledge is no longer scarce; it's scattered. The next challenge is to build systems that translate information abundance into behavioral competence.

title: Between Solidarity and Concern: Refugee Inflow and Crime Perception
affiliations: Universitat de València and University of Tübingen

detail.title: Between Solidarity and Concern: Refugee Inflow and Crime Perception
detail.abstract: Most empirical research finds that immigration has no effect on crime. Nevertheless, public concerns about immigration and crime persist, possibly driven by misperceptions. In this paper, we examine how an immigration shock affects crime perception. Specifically, we analyze the impact of the sudden and large-scale arrival of Ukrainian refugees in Poland following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Using unique data on reported safety concerns, we find a persistent decline in perceived risk in regions more affected by the refugee inflow. We provide additional evidence that this effect stems from a shift in local crime perception due to exposure to war refugees, rather than from a reduction in actual safety threats.

title: Can Tax Incentives Act as Catalysts for a Circular Economy? Modeling Tax Strategies to Drive Circular Innovation
affiliations: Arkansas State University

detail.title: Can Tax Incentives Act as Catalysts for a Circular Economy? Modeling Tax Strategies to Drive Circular Innovation
detail.abstract: This chapter investigates how tax incentives can influence firm-level investment in circular economy practices under environmental regulatory constraints. Motivated by the rising policy emphasis on fiscal instruments to support sustainable transitions, the study develops an analytical optimization model of a representative firm that faces a regulatory waste cap and may invest in circular practices to reduce environmental penalties. The model integrates production costs, environmental externalities, tax incentives, and the convex costs of sustainable investment. Through a constrained nonlinear optimization and numerical experiment simulation, the study identifies key behavioral patterns: (1) a critical activation threshold of tax incentives below which firms remain inactive; (2) a coupling effect whereby production and circular investment rise together to satisfy waste regulations; and (3) saturation and metastability effects as investment costs and waste-reduction returns flatten. A case study of the German packaging sector illustrates the model's real-world relevance.

title: The Inelasticity Shift a Market-Level Theory of Sexual Access After Liberalization
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: The Inelasticity Shift a Market-Level Theory of Sexual Access After Liberalization
detail.abstract: This paper develops a market-based theory of contemporary intimacy that treats sexual access and relational commitment as distinct goods governed by different elasticities, costs and signaling mechanisms. It argues that sexual liberalization and digital matching platforms produced a structural supply shock that transformed sexual access from a high elasticity good into an inelastic one, while relational commitment became hyperelastic under heightened volatility. The analysis introduces three core parameters. The elasticity of relational access (ERA) captures how changes in overall investment affect sexual access outcomes. Linguistic signal efficiency (LSE) measures the marginal impact of linguistic investment on access and is shown to collapse under conditions of liquidity and noise. The volatility adjusted linguistic cost (VALC) formalizes how high market volatility inflates the cost of producing credible commitments. Drawing on communication theory, signaling theory and formal work on syntactic autonomy, the paper frames language as a signaling market that has shifted from scarcity to oversupply, degrading the informational value of discourse. Sexual access becomes insensitive to marginal changes in investment, while commitment becomes highly sensitive to small increases in perceived risk. The result is a dual elastic market in which low tier, template language governs access, and high competence linguistic forms operate as filters for long term partner selection. This framework offers a structural, non-moral account of post liberalization relationship markets and provides testable parameters for future empirical research.

title: Is Artificial Intelligence (AI) Changing the Way We Do Economics?

detail.title: Is Artificial Intelligence (AI) Changing the Way We Do Economics?

detail.abstract: This paper presents a review of how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way we study and practice economics. It explores how new generations of academics, researchers, and students in economics will face new challenges and need to adapt to emerging technologies such as AI. At the same time, it highlights a potential decline in human intellectual performance and an increasing dependency on AI. This study evaluates how AI may influence the creation of new and innovative knowledge in economics while simultaneously contributing to a reduction in human-generated research output. Furthermore, it emphasizes the weakening capacity of humans to independently solve complex and dynamic economic problems. The growing reliance on AI in daily life is expected to become so pervasive that it could eventually influence even the smallest individual and collective decisions. Hence, this paper presents a theoretical analysis supporting the argument that AI may become a destroyer of intellectual creativity and critical thinking in solving complex economic problems a development that could prove irreversible. Additionally, the same research proposes a simple methodology for using artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots in the construction of economic models. It outlines, step by step, how to systematically build an economic model with the support of an AI chatbot such as ChatGPT. This new methodology, called Artificial Intelligence Economic Models Prototyping (AIEM-Prototyping), offers a transformative approach to teaching, learning, and researching economics from a methodological perspective. The process begins with the manual creation of a basic prototype, which is then enhanced through the integration of AI chatbots to evaluate and analyse economic phenomena. AIEM-Prototyping shifts economics from being primarily a theoretical discipline toward a more practical and applied science capable of explaining and simulating dynamic socioeconomic systems through realistic representations. Today, it is possible to create, evaluate, and simulate economic problems using real images or videos generated with ChatGPT. This enables faster comprehension and facilitates the identification of efficient and feasible solutions. Ultimately, AIEM-Prototyping can be applied across all areas of economics, including microeconomics, macroeconomics, applied economics, economic thought, finance, banking, management, business economics, and other related fields.

title: Tourism as a Driver of Economic Transformation: Pathways Toward Sustainable and Inclusive Growth in the Maldives
affiliations: and University of Puerto Rico

detail.title: Tourism as a Driver of Economic Transformation: Pathways Toward Sustainable and Inclusive Growth in the Maldives
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of tourism as a catalyst for economic transformation in the Maldives, a small island developing state where tourism constitutes the backbone of national income, employment, and foreign exchange. Over the past four decades, the sector has evolved from a luxury niche market into a diversified and resilient component of the Maldivian economy. Drawing on policy analysis, institutional reports, and comparative evidence, the study explores how tourism has driven infrastructure expansion, human capital development, and regional integration. It also highlights the growing emphasis on sustainability and inclusiveness as core pillars of national development strategies. The findings suggest that while tourism has successfully propelled economic growth, it also poses environmental and social challenges-ranging from ecosystem degradation to spatial inequality. The paper argues that achieving long-term resilience requires embedding green innovation, local empowerment, and climate adaptation into the tourism model. The Maldivian case provides valuable insights into how small economies can leverage tourism for sustainable and inclusive transformation in a globalized world.

title: Cultural Drivers of Economic Outcomes: Cross-Societal Evidence and Comparative Insights

detail.title: Cultural Drivers of Economic Outcomes: Cross-Societal Evidence and Comparative Insights
detail.abstract: Culture profoundly influences how societies organize work, value cooperation, and pursue economic progress. This paper explores how shared beliefs, values, and social norms shape economic outcomes across diverse societies. Drawing on comparative international evidence, it examines the connections between cultural orientations-such as trust, individualism, and long-term thinking-and national patterns of productivity, innovation, and governance. The discussion highlights that economic performance cannot be explained by institutions and resources alone; cultural attitudes toward cooperation, responsibility, and change play a crucial role in sustaining development. Through a crosssocietal perspective, the study illustrates how cultural adaptability fosters innovation and resilience, while rigid or hierarchical traditions may limit growth. Ultimately, the paper argues that successful development strategies must recognize culture not as a background condition but as an active, evolving force that shapes economic behavior and collective prosperity.

title: Equatorial Economies in a Warming World: Climate Challenges and Adaptive Futures
affiliations: Independent and OPGS University, India

detail.title: Equatorial Economies in a Warming World: Climate Challenges and Adaptive Futures
detail.abstract: This paper examines the unique climate-related challenges and adaptive trajectories of equatorial economies in an era of global warming. Concentrated around the Earth's midline, these nations face intensifying heat, erratic rainfall, and ecosystem stress that directly influence agriculture, health, and economic stability. The study explores how climatic variability intersects with structural vulnerabilities such as dependence on natural resources, limited industrial diversification, and demographic pressures. Drawing on comparative evidence from Africa, Southeast Asia, and Latin America, it highlights the uneven capacity of equatorial states to adapt to environmental change. While some countries are advancing green infrastructure, climate-smart agriculture, and renewable energy transitions, others remain constrained by governance and resource gaps. The paper argues that sustainable futures for equatorial economies depend on integrating climate adaptation into development planning, fostering regional cooperation, and leveraging indigenous knowledge to build resilience in a warming world.

title: Tourism and Economic Resilience: Rethinking Growth in an Era of Global Interdependence
affiliations: Independent and University of Puerto Rico, School of Law, Students

detail.title: Tourism and Economic Resilience: Rethinking Growth in an Era of Global Interdependence
detail.abstract: This paper explores the evolving role of tourism as a driver of economic resilience in an era of increasing global interdependence. As international connectivity deepens, tourism has emerged not only as a source of income and employment but also as a mechanism for economic diversification, regional stability, and cultural exchange. Drawing on comparative evidence from both developed and developing economies, the study examines how tourism supports recovery from external shocks-such as pandemics, financial crises, and environmental disruptions-by stimulating local entrepreneurship and sustaining value chains. The analysis highlights the dual nature of tourism: while it enhances adaptive capacity and innovation, it also exposes economies to global volatility and environmental stress. The paper argues that rethinking growth through the lens of resilience requires integrating sustainability, inclusiveness, and digital transformation into tourism policy. Such an approach can position tourism as a cornerstone of balanced and future-oriented economic development.

title: Estimating Time-Variation in Matching Efficiency and Match Elasticity for the US Labor Market
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: Estimating Time-Variation in Matching Efficiency and Match Elasticity for the US Labor Market
detail.abstract: The paper estimates time-varying matching efficiency and match elasticity within a Cobb-Douglas matching function for the U.S. non-farm sector, using a state-space model. It evaluates two specifications: (i) no constant returns to scale (CRS) with time variation (my baseline model) and (ii) CRS with time variation. We compare these two models with the standard model without time variability, and the results show significant time variation in both parameters, even under stochastic volatility. Counterfactual vacancy estimates reveal that the non-CRS baseline model fits the data best. This model suggests a gradual decline in matching efficiency, indicating growing labor market inefficiencies. Matching efficiency and match elasticity with respect to unemployment are found to be procyclical. The procyclicality in efficiency can be attributed to reduced sectoral reallocation, as seen in CPS data, driven by structural economic shifts. Procyclical match elasticity points to the nonlinear effect of labor market tightness on the job-finding rate. The paper also finds a rise in the efficient unemployment rate after COVID-19, as estimated by the baseline model.

detail.abstract: Public subsidies for methane mitigation infrastructure aim to combat climate change, but they may perversely incentivize polluting industries' growth. title: Beyond Stated Preferences: Tacit Consensus as Cultural Lock-in in Institutional Reform

detail.title: Beyond Stated Preferences: Tacit Consensus as Cultural Lock-in in Institutional Reform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, professional, or personal relationships that could constitute conflicts of interest regarding this research. The author has no affiliations with labor unions, business associations, political parties, or government bodies that could influence or be perceived to influence this study. This research was conducted independently without external funding or institutional support. All data sources used are publicly available (presidential speeches, legislative records, survey data from Latinobarómetro, Poliarquía, and Universidad Torcuato Di Tella). The conceptual inspiration for "tacit consensus" comes from Alejandro Poli Gonzalvo's essay "La era del consenso tácito" (Revista Seúl, November 2025), which is appropriately cited throughout the paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patients, or experimental interventions. The research analyzes publicly available secondary data (presidential speeches, legislative records, published survey results) and does not require ethics approval. No primary data collection involving human subjects was conducted. declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted independently by the author without financial support.

detail.abstract:
Institutional reform theories conventionally measure popular support through explicit preferences—surveys, electoral mandates, crisis urgency. Yet Argentina exhibits a paradox: 71% public support for labor flexibility reforms coexists with 0% reform success over 33 years (23 failed attempts, 1991-2024). This paper introduces cultural lock-in (CLI_cultural) as measurable constraint operating below conscious awareness, overriding stated preferences through tacit consensus.

I operationalize CLI_cultural via three behavioral indicators: (1) CT1 (narrative stability): discourse convergence across ideologically opposed governments, (2) CT2 (shock resistance): semantic invariance following exogenous crises, (3) CT3 (policy continuity): behavioral patterns unchanged despite electoral mandates.

Comparative analysis of Argentina (CLI=0.81, range 0.78-0.84), Uruguay (0.68, range 0.65-0.71), and Chile (0.45, range 0.42-0.48) demonstrates CLI_cultural aligns with reform capacity better than veto players, survey preferences, or economic crises.

In non-WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic; Henrich et al. 2010) contexts, implicit behavioral consensus systematically diverges from explicit stated preferences, producing institutional paralysis despite overwhelming reform support. 

I specify differentiated reform strategies calibrated to CLI_cultural levels: cultural erosion for high lock-in contexts (8-17 year timeline), incremental coalitions for moderate contexts, direct reform for low contexts.

title: Evaluating Online Exercise Solution Videos Versus a Detailed Explanation in Class Using Data on Students’ Learning and Repetition Behavior

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We conduct a field experiment to analyze whether online exercise solution videos are a valuable substitute for a detailed explanation in class. Using a Difference-in-Difference identification strategy with student time-fixed effects, we find that videos on-demand reduce students' performance significantly. Splitting our sample along class attendance shows that the results are driven by those students, who attended class. Given our detailed data on students' learning and repetition behavior we can show that only one out of four students in the treatment group watched the videos while four out of five students in the control group attended the respective class. Although we observe the typical procrastination behavior among students as the exam approaches we find no evidence that procrastination in the experiment questions compared with all other exercise questions is higher for students in the treatment group compared to the control group.

title: Linear Regressions with Combined Data
affiliations: Center for Research in Economics and Statistics (CREST),  and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Linear Regressions with Combined Data

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study linear regressions in a context where the outcome of interest and some of the covariates are observed in two different datasets that cannot be matched. Traditional approaches obtain point identification by relying, often implicitly, on exclusion restrictions. We show that without such restrictions, coefficients of interest can still be partially identified, with the sharp bounds taking a simple form. We obtain tighter bounds when variables observed in both datasets, but not included in the regression of interest, are available, even if these variables are not subject to specific restrictions. We develop computationally simple and asymptotically normal estimators of the bounds. Finally, we apply our methodology to estimate racial disparities in patent approval rates and to evaluate the effect of patience and risk-taking on educational performance.

title: Critical Analysis of Applicable Legal Regulation of Plastic and Hazardous Waste in Bangladesh

detail.title: Critical Analysis of Applicable Legal Regulation of Plastic and Hazardous Waste in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: This study looks at Bangladesh's laws governing plastic and hazardous waste, emphasizing the serious risks they pose to the environment and public health. Enforcement is still lax and dispersed even though the nation was the first to outlaw thin plastic bags in 2002 and passed important legislation like the Environment Conservation Act of 1995, the Medical Waste Management Rules of 2008, and the Solid Waste Management Rules of 2021. Although there has been progress in Bangladesh's alignment with international instruments such as the Basel and Stockholm Conventions, the country remains vulnerable due to gaps in ratification, monitoring, and compliance, especially in the shipbreaking and e-waste sectors. Stronger legal responses have been pushed for by judicial activism, particularly through historic BELA cases; however, institutional flaws, corruption, and low public awareness make implementation difficult. The study also looks at the necessity of integrating informal waste workers into formal systems, the role of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), and regional cooperation under SAARC and BIMSTEC. It ends with suggestions for a thorough waste law, more robust enforcement tactics, financial rewards for environmentally friendly substitutes, and increased public involvement. For Bangladesh to achieve sustainable waste management and environmental protection, it is imperative that legal frameworks and governance capacity be strengthened.

title: Understanding the Energy–Water–Socioeconomic Nexus in E-7 Economies: Evidence from a Panel QARDL Framework

detail.title: Understanding the Energy–Water–Socioeconomic Nexus in E-7 Economies: Evidence from a Panel QARDL Framework
detail.abstract: This study explores the interconnections between energy consumption, water productivity, and socioeconomic factors in the E-7 economies (Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Russia, and Turkey) over the period 1997–2022. The research aims to identify how macroeconomic stability, demographic dynamics, and energy use jointly influence water-use efficiency within the framework of sustainable development. Using the Panel Quantile Autoregressive Distributed Lag (QARDL) model, the study captures heterogeneous and asymmetric dynamics across conditional quantiles of water productivity, allowing both short- and long-run relationships to vary by performance level. The empirical results reveal that electricity consumption exerts a consistently positive and significant effect on water productivity across all quantiles, whereas inflation and fertility have limited impacts. Economic growth and trade openness show diverse, quantile-specific patterns, reflecting structural differences among the E-7 countries. The findings confirm a stable long-run cointegration relationship among the variables. Overall, the study provides new empirical evidence that enhancing energy efficiency, promoting renewable energy, and implementing quantile-specific sustainability policies are essential to achieving balanced progress toward Sustainable Development Goals 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) in emerging economies.

title: Investor Attention, Microstructure Noise and Crude Oil Market Volatility
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Investor Attention, Microstructure Noise and Crude Oil Market Volatility
detail.abstract: Geopolitical tensions, exemplified by the Russia–Ukraine conflict, have intensified uncertainty and volatility in global crude oil markets. This study develops an extended Heterogeneous Autoregressive (HAR) model to investigate the effects of investor attention and microstructure noise on crude oil market volatility, which is estimated from ultra-high-frequency data by the pre-averaging method. The empirical results demonstrate: (i) Microstructure noise drives significant in-sample short horizons volatility in both crude oil futures and fund markets but exhibits divergent predictive utility out-of-sample, enhancing forecasting accuracy for futures volatility while yielding no improvement for fund volatility. (ii) Investor attention, proxied by the Google Search Volume Index, exhibits heterogeneous effects between the crude oil fund and crude oil futures. It exerts a significant positive impact on fund volatility, while its negative effect on futures volatility remains insignificant. These findings are valuable for energy derivatives pricing, cross-market hedging strategies, and real-time monitoring of systemic risks in the commodity market.

title: Construction of a Survival Time Purchasing Power Model and Cross-National Comparative Research: A New Perspective Based on the Material Comparison Method
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Construction of a Survival Time Purchasing Power Model and Cross-National Comparative Research: A New Perspective Based on the Material Comparison Method
detail.abstract: This study aims to construct an innovative model termed "Survival Time Purchasing Power" (STPP) to quantitatively compare the real survival efficiency of minimum-income earners under different welfare regimes. The core model is: Survival Time (hours) = Benchmark Hourly Wage / ((Basic Living Cost + Risk Reserve) / 720). To address the challenge of cross-national data comparability, this study proposes the "Material Comparison Method," which assesses and selects comparable data from China, Germany, and Japan based on physical dimensions such as nutritional intake and housing conditions. Empirical calculations show that the "survival time" for Germany, Japan, and China is 14.12 hours, 8.94 hours, and 4.18 hours, respectively, indicating significant disparities. This gap primarily stems from the extent to which respective social welfare systems 分担 (share) the individual's "Risk Reserve" (measured by per capita out-of-pocket health expenditure), rather than from nominal income levels. This study not only provides a novel analytical tool for micro-level welfare comparison but also offers an effective methodological path, the "Material Comparison Method," to resolve the problem of crossnational data incomparability. The research confirms that the welfare system, through its risksharing mechanism, profoundly reshapes an individual's survival efficiency as a form of "social wage.

title: A General Effective-Parameter Principle for Linear PDEs with Random Coefficients
affiliations: University of the West Indies (UWI)

detail.title: A General Effective-Parameter Principle for Linear PDEs with Random Coefficients
detail.abstract: We develop a general and exact representation theorem for linear partial differential equations (PDEs) whose coefficients depend on a finite-dimensional random parameter. Under minimal assumptions---continuity of the solution with respect to the parameter and compactness/connectedness of the parameter domain---the unconditional solution of such a random-parameter PDE coincides, pointwise, with the deterministic solution evaluated at a suitable effective parameter. The result is non-asymptotic, does not rely on homogenization, ergodicity, or scale separation, and applies to linear parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, fractional, and integro-differential equations. We present a fully expanded introduction, an extended literature review, strengthened proofs (including functional-analytic and semigroup-based arguments), measurable selection and regularity results for the effective parameter, and explicit examples. We also relate the principle to classical stochastic homogenization, uncertainty quantification, and random operator theory.

title: Reassessing the Strength of Industrial Banks: Evidence, Trends, and Policy Implications

detail.abstract: Industrial banks (IB) are state-chartered, FDIC-insured institutions that commercial or financial parents may own, and they occupy a distinctive niche in the U.S. banking system. We document that IBs differ from other FDIC-insured banks along three core margins: (i) ownership and supervision (CALMA/PCA commitments that contractually obligate parents to act as sources of strength), (ii) business models (specialized, often nationally distributed lending with heavy use of brokered deposits), and (iii) performance and resilience. From 2000 to 2025, we demonstrate that IBs-especially those with commercial parents-exhibit persistently higher ROA/ROE and stronger capitalization than other banks. Critically, this exists even during the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 shock. IB funding relies disproportionately on (insured) brokered deposits and higher capitalization. As a result, IB failures are rare and small in aggregate relative to the broader system. IBs have niche business models that lead them to decrease market concentration and enable them to increase product innovation. Their market segments focus on specialized and underserved segments, often using information advantages from their parent company. We discuss the policy tradeoffs of layering additional regulation onto a framework in which FDIC/state oversight already mirrors that of comparable banks. We find little evidence that restrictions on commercial ownership would deliver stability benefits, but that they could increase compliance and innovation costs.

title: Intraseasonal Variations in Time Use, Food Security, and Health Outcomes among Women in Rural Malawi ✻
