detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer a laboratory experiment; it is a boardroom mandate. This paper sits at the crossroads of enterprise AI strategy, operational efficiency, and governance, offering leaders a blueprint for aligning technology investments with measurable business outcomes. Large Language Models (LLMs), while technically impressive, are expensive, slow, and often incompatible with compliance and ESG objectives. Enterprises face ballooning compute costs, energy usage that contradicts sustainability commitments, and regulatory risk from shipping sensitive data to public clouds. These barriers slow deployment and erode ROI, turning AI into a cost center rather than a growth driver. This paper argues that Small Language Models (SLMs), when combined with deep domain knowledge and a hybrid architecture that escalates to LLMs only, when necessary, can unlock transformative value. The philosophy mirrors the evolution from centralized mainframes to decentralized computing in the PC era, where smaller, distributed systems created faster and more flexible business outcomes. We also explore risks, including the Cobra Effect, Goodhart's Law, and the Lucas Critique, as applied to AI adoption, ensuring leaders can navigate tradeoffs responsibly. Results from early adopters are striking; latency falls to milliseconds, infrastructure costs drop sharply, and regulator confidence improves. This approach enables executives to turn AI into a scalable, governance-aligned capability that accelerates transformation instead of slowing it down.

title: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Explaining Professional Boundary Dynamics

detail.title: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Explaining Professional Boundary Dynamics
detail.abstract: Professions are dynamic social structures whose jurisdictional boundaries are continually drawn, contested, and redrawn. Existing accounts in sociology, organizational studies, and history richly describe these processes but often lack micro-foundations that make the mechanisms transparent and comparable across settings. This paper proposes a game-theoretic framework to analyze professional boundary change as strategic interaction among practitioner groups, using accounting as the primary empirical context. This paper models merger (boundary elimination) and split (boundary construction) as outcomes of coalition formation (cooperation) versus noncooperation, with payoffs shaped by market revenues (MKT), avoidable operating costs (CST), and non-economic benefits (NEB) such as identity, autonomy, and status. Four games escalate in complexity: (1) two players in one market, (2) three players in one market, (3) three players across a regulated and an unregulated market, and (4) two players with differential growth and per-member payoffs. The framework formalizes conditions for individually rational (IR) merger, examines when transferable utility (TU) enables otherwise infeasible cooperation, and clarifies how external threats, regulation, branding spillovers, and growth alter equilibrium outcomes. This paper also discusses governance, government intervention, international bodies, and nested market power within a profession. The framework offers accounting scholars a portable analytic tool for diagnosing merger feasibility, explaining persistence of fragmentation, and designing policy levers that work by changing game parameters rather than imposing outcomes. This paper conclude with implications, contributions, and limitations, including challenges in empirically measuring expected market shifts and the rarity of clean merger events for testing.

detail.abstract: The transition from school to the labor market presents significant challenges. This is particularly the case in low- and middle-income countries where the youth population attending primary and secondary school is expanding rapidly and overoptimism combined with limited information can lead to suboptimal decision-making regarding further education and other career preparation choices. We design and test through a cluster-randomized controlled trial a scalable low-cost intervention designed to help secondary school students in Tanzania develop hopeful yet realistic career plans. This is done through a structured, edutainment podcast series and teacher-led classroom discussions. We show that treated students perform better academically, with a significant increase in national exam success and a higher likelihood of selection into further education. Additionally, self-employment rates and income levels increase. These outcomes are plausibly driven by enhanced hope—characterized by improved agency and pathway clarity—, by an increase in the likelihood of developing b-plans, and by a reduction in stress. Our findings highlight the potential of structured guidance through edutainment in improving the transition from secondary school.

title: Beyond Ownership: Indigenous Stewardship as Framework for Post-Scarcity Constitutionalism

detail.title: Beyond Ownership: Indigenous Stewardship as Framework for Post-Scarcity Constitutionalism
detail.abstract: This paper reframes debates about Indigenous sovereignty and constitutional legitimacy in postcolonial nations by examining the functional obsolescence of European ownership models in emerging post-scarcity conditions. Drawing on Ostrom's (1990) Nobel Prize-winning principles of commons governance and the formal repudiation of the Doctrine of Discovery (Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace, 2023; UN Human Rights Council, 2021), we contend that Indigenous stewardship frameworks represent not historical artefacts but sophisticated legal systems optimally suited for abundance management. Quantitative evidence demonstrates that Indigenous-managed lands exhibit superior ecological outcomes compared to protected areas (Fa et al., 2020; Schuster et al., 2019). Constitutional recognition of Indigenous sovereignty is presented as a positive-sum transition from the failing logic of the scarcity-based Extraction Paradigm (market/state binary) to the proven effectiveness of the Stewardship Paradigm. This analysis shows that legal continuity arguments cannot resolve foundational legitimacy deficits when the underlying dominant epistemic architecture actively obstructs human flourishing in conditions of technological potential and ecological urgency.

detail.abstract:
Botswana stands at a strategic inflection point as global sustainability expectations intensify and capital markets shift toward ESG-aligned transparency. Long recognised for governance stability and macroeconomic discipline, the country now faces increasing investor scrutiny amid climate vulnerability, sectoral concentration risks, and a historic political transition in 2024. Using ESG GPS®, Africa’s first AI-powered sustainability analytics platform, this study provides a data-driven assessment of ESG disclosure maturity across companies listed on the Botswana Stock Exchange (BSE). The analysis shows strong governance transparency, emerging but uneven social reporting, and early-stage environmental disclosure—particularly regarding emissions, energy use, and net-zero commitments.

These findings are contextualised within Botswana’s evolving sustainability architecture, including recent policy reforms, strengthened financial-reporting regulations, and the government’s introduction of carbon-market and carbon-pricing mechanisms. As Botswana positions itself for participation in global carbon and nature-based markets, credible measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems will become central to its competitiveness. The study highlights how robust ESG disclosure and carbon-accounting practices can support Botswana’s economic diversification agenda, mitigate concentration risks in diamonds, cattle, coal, and tourism, and unlock new revenue streams from high-integrity carbon markets.

The results point to a country structurally prepared for ESG integration but still at an early stage of environmental alignment. Strengthening ESG transparency—supported by national policy momentum and investor expectations—offers Botswana a pathway to green industrialisation, improved capital-market resilience, and sustainable development. This paper contributes to African ESG scholarship by providing the first integrated, platform-based assessment of Botswana’s corporate sustainability landscape and its implications for future competitiveness.

title: Utilization of Vinegar and Soap as a Natural Herbicide Alternative for Weed Control in Oil Palm Plantations

detail.title: Utilization of Vinegar and Soap as a Natural Herbicide Alternative for Weed Control in Oil Palm Plantations
detail.abstract: Weeds represent one of the primary constraints in oil palm cultivation, as they significantly reduce crop yield and overall plant quality. Conventional chemical herbicides are widely used for weed suppression; however, their long-term application poses substantial environmental and human health risks. This study aims to investigate the potential use of vinegar and soap as a natural, environmentally friendly herbicide alternative for weed control in oil palm plantations. A field experiment was conducted using various concentrations of vinegar (60%, 70%, and 80%) combined with liquid soap as an adjuvant. The results revealed that the 60% vinegar-soap formulation demonstrated the highest effectiveness, reducing weed populations by up to 90% within seven days after application. Cost analysis further indicated that the vinegar-soap mixture significantly lowered per-cap spraying costs compared with conventional chemical herbicides. These findings confirm that natural herbicides based on vinegar and soap are not only effective but also environmentally sustainable, offering a promising strategy to reduce dependence on chemical herbicides that may cause ecological degradation and health hazards.

detail.title: Current levels vs. longitudinal changes: A 7-year study on physical function, brain structure and cognition in older adults
detail.abstract: Background Declines in physical function, brain structure, and cognition are common effects of aging in later life. Here we investigate whether changes in physical function and gray matter volumes over a seven-year span predict cognitive performance in older adults. Methods We analyzed five assessments of physical function and MRI-derived gray matter volumes in 219 older adults (mean age 73.7, SD = 2.5). We applied Bayesian linear regression models and model averaging to examine their associations with cognitive performance. We deemed associations meaningful if the inclusion Bayes factor (BFinclusion) was 3 or higher. Results Long-term memory performance was associated with current grip strength with moderate evidence (BFinclusion= 3.52). Additionally, there was moderate evidence for a relationship between hippocampal decline over time and both cognitive processing speed (BFinclusion = 4.87), and executive functioning (BFinclusion = 5.34), although these associations became anecdotal when removing extreme values. Remaining physical function measures and brain volumes yielded only anecdotal evidence for or against predicting cognitive function. Conclusions These findings provide moderate evidence that indices of current physical function and longitudinal measures of brain structure are predictive of cognitive abilities in older adults. This indicates a need for monitoring brain structure over time to characterize its relationship with cognitive function. Additionally, a global measure of physical function, such as grip strength, may serve as an indicator of a person’s long-term memory, even when measured at only a single time point. These tentative findings motivate replication attempts in larger samples.

detail.title: When Research Stigmatizes the Researcher: Navigating Reputational Challenges in Researching Transgender People's (Taboo) Lives
detail.abstract:
Background: While research is seen as a noble pursuit that elevates the status of scholars, little attention has been paid to the reputational risks it may pose, particularly in culturally conservative contexts. 
Aim: Some topics are so sensitive culturally (referred to in this article as taboo topics) that engaging with them as a researcher is met with social discomfort and disapproval. This study explores whether and how sensitive social research damages the reputation of researchers. 

Methods: It focuses on the research experiences of six cisgender scholars who conducted fieldwork with transgender communities in Pakistan. 

Results: The findings reveal that research posed risks to the researchers, rendering them socially vulnerable and susceptible to reputational harm. To navigate these risks, they deployed short-term strategies such as carefully selecting the timing and location of interactions and modifying their appearance to avoid suspicion. Over the long term, they engaged in selective disclosure, offering emotional and intellectual justifications to close contacts or concealing the nature of their research entirely. 

Conclusion: The research concludes that working on sensitive taboo topics can harm the researcher's reputation. Furthermore, the researchers' experiences and their strategies reflect the complex ethical and social terrain that researchers must navigate, highlighting how reputational concerns deter engagement with marginalized topics and contribute to their continued neglect in academic and policy domains.

title: The Value-Web Advantage: Governing Legitimacy, Fairness, and Resilience

detail.title: The Value-Web Advantage: Governing Legitimacy, Fairness, and Resilience
detail.abstract: The Value-Web Advantage: Governing Legitimacy, Fairness, and Resilience reframes strategic management for an era defined by interdependence, stakeholder activism, and systemic complexity. Traditional strategy models—such as Porter’s Five Forces, the Value Stick, and Playing to Win—focus on competition and efficiency but overlook the legitimacy and fairness required for long-term ecosystem health. The Value-Web Strategy (VWS) offers a new grammar and logic flow that positions strategy as stewardship rather than rivalry. Anchored in four theoretical pillars—Stakeholder Theory, Institutional Theory, Complex Adaptive Systems, and Service-Dominant Logic—the framework integrates moral, social, and systemic dimensions of value creation. It introduces four diagnostic metrics—MAV (Minimum Acceptable Value), PVD (Perceived Value Delivered), FVD (Fairness of Value Distribution), and EVS (Ecosystem Value Score)—to measure legitimacy and trust across interconnected actors. The VWS 7-Step Playbook (Define → Map → Diagnose → Analyze → Craft → Govern → Renew) provides a structured process for aligning purpose, governance, and renewal across firms, governments, and civil society. By bridging conceptual depth with practical tools, this white paper advances a model for sustainable advantage in complex ecosystems—one where legitimacy becomes currency, fairness becomes infrastructure, and resilience becomes the defining measure of strategic success.

detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the fiscal implications of federal permitting reform in U.S. infrastructure policy. Using project-level data from the Council on Environmental Quality's (CEQ) Permitting Dashboard (Council on Environment Quality 2025), this paper estimates that FAST-41 coverage reduces median federal permitting timelines by approximately two years relative to non-FAST projects. The analysis applies discounted cash-flow models to representative federal revenue streams and finds that each year that avoided delays preserved between $50 and $200 million in present-value fiscal receipts per project. Aggregate effects were found to be in the multi-billion-dollar range. Sectoral calibrations using ONRR, EIA, and FERC data (U.S. Department of the Interior, Office of Natural Resources Revenue 2024; U.S. Energy Information Administration 2024; Federal Energy Regulatory Commission 2024) indicate that pipelines, transmission lines, and renewable projects yielded particularly large fiscal dividends. The findings, ultimately, show that streamlining permitting can strengthen both administrative performance and the federal fiscal position in a way that creates budgetary capacity without broad-based tax increase.

The book provides a comprehensive overview of the tools used within the political economy of communication (PEC) field, including quantitative, qualitative, and emerging digital methodologies. Each section explores essential PEC methods, statistical and network analysis, ethnographic research, discourse analysis, and digital ethnography, revealing both their potential and limitations. The article highlights the importance of these methodologies in understanding the complex power structures and social dynamics that define media systems, particularly in the digital era. While the volume excels in contextualizing PEC within broader social science frameworks, this review also addresses gaps in advanced quantitative applications and practical AI integration. Overall, the book's methodological insights offer valuable resources for both seasoned scholars and newcomers, enriching the discourse on media and communication research's evolving landscape.

detail.title: Acceptability in Context: A Multidimensional Analysis of Urine-Based HPV Screening in Rural Eswatini
detail.abstract:
Background: Acceptability is a critical factor in access to healthcare, shaping individuals’ engagement with preventive services and interventions, but it is often conceptualized as mere willingness. This study examines the acceptability of urine-based cervical cancer screening in a rural healthcare setting in Eswatini, focusing on both women’s and healthcare providers’ perspectives. 

Methods: A mixed-methods approach was used, including semi-structured interviews with women, focus group discussions with health workers, teachers and outreach staff, and a survey among women and girls attending a rural clinic. This approach offered a nuanced understanding of how cultural norms, individual attitudes, and structural barriers shaped perceptions of HPV screening. 

Results: Urine-based screening was highly acceptable (99%), with participants overwhelmingly preferring it to invasive methods such as Pap smear or VIA. The ease, privacy, and non-invasiveness of the test were consistently appreciated by participants. At the same time stigma, misinformation, and local understandings of cervical cancer screening shaped behaviours, potentially limiting demand or fuelling fears. These factors did not necessarily prevent initial acceptance but may influence long-term adherence and community uptake. Healthcare providers play a pivotal role in building trust and encouraging participation through their engagement and sense of ownership. 

Conclusion: Urine-based HPV screening proved to be more than acceptable in this rural Eswatini setting, offering a feasible and welcomed alternative to conventional methods. Understanding social and systemic factors is crucial for developing culturally responsive and sustainable screening programs that reduce barriers and support informed, long-term participation.

title: Towards Explainable AI–Driven Individualized Treatment Optimization for Breast Cancer Time-to-Event Outcomes

detail.title: Towards Explainable AI–Driven Individualized Treatment Optimization for Breast Cancer Time-to-Event Outcomes
detail.abstract: Individualized treatment optimization remains a major challenge in healthcare, and its applications in breast cancer are still limited. This study introduces a computational framework that integrates survival analysis with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for individualized treatment selection based on time-to-event outcomes in breast cancer patients, providing a solution to support personalized care. Machine learning survival models—including Random Survival Forests (RSF), DeepSurv, DeepHit, Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH), and XGBoost with an accelerated failure time (XGBoost-AFT)—were trained to estimate individualized survival probabilities under two treatment strategies: surgery alone (S-Only) and multimodal therapy (MultiTx). Predictive performance was assessed using the concordance index (C-index) and integrated brier score (IBS), while treatment selection was evaluated by comparing Kaplan–Meier survival between model-concordant and model-discordant patient groups. DeepHit achieved the highest predictive accuracy with 20 features (C-index 0.85, IBS 0.072), whereas RSF demonstrated the strongest discrimination for 10-year survival and provided statistically significant stratification of outcomes in both treatment groups. In contrast, the CoxPH model consistently assigned all patients to the MultiTx group, indicating a lack of discriminatory power for individualized treatment selection. Model explainability with SHAP analysis identified routinely collected clinical features, such as tumor stage, histology, and comorbidity burden, as key predictors, consistent with established clinical knowledge and revealing treatment-specific patterns. Overall, these findings demonstrate that explainable survival-based machine learning can effectively support individualized treatment optimization in breast cancer, establishing a foundation for time-to-event–driven, patient-centered decision support in clinical practice.

detail.abstract: This study examined the influence of cultural context and linguistic proximity on bilateral trade using a modified gravity model. The analysis incorporated trade data from 117 countries, encompassing 6,623 bilateral trading relationships. Bilateral trade was modeled as a function of cultural context, linguistic proximity, and other relevant economic and geographic factors. The results suggested that linguistic proximity does not appear to have a statistically significant effect on bilateral trade when evaluating total trade. However, the findings support the notion that cultural context distance plays a role in promoting trade. Specifically, sharing the same cultural context was associated with reduced bilateral trade, whereas greater cultural context distance between trading partners appeared to enhance trade.

detail.title: Economic Recovery and Inequality in Post-Disaster Housing: A Case Study of Paradise, California's 2018 Camp Fire
detail.abstract: Natural disasters are often described as great equalizers, yet their aftermath reveals sharp social and economic divides. This study examines the post-disaster economic recovery of Paradise, California, following the 2018 Camp Fire, the deadliest wildfire in the state's history. Using publicly available datasets including the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI), American Community Survey (ACS), local building permits, and county assessor data, this paper investigates disparities in recovery rates between high-value and low-value residential areas. The findings demonstrate that affluent neighborhoods recovered faster and achieved higher reconstruction rates, while lower-income and affordable housing sectors experienced prolonged displacement and limited rebuilding. These outcomes provide empirical support for theories of 'recovery machines' and 'disaster gentrification,' emphasizing the intersection of wealth, insurance access, and policy design in shaping resilience trajectories. By situating the Paradise case within a broader literature on urban inequality and environmental risk, the research contributes to ongoing debates on how planning institutions can balance rapid recovery with social justice. The results underline the need for integrated policy mechanisms that ensure both structural safety and equity in post-disaster environments.

detail.abstract:
Background: Field experiment was conducted under In-house Project of the University during kharif seasons of 2015 and 2017 for evaluation of clusterbean varieties for Koshi Region of Bihar. 

Methods: The experiment was conducted by using randomized complete block design with three replications. Observations were recorded on different agronomic parameters including, plant height, dry matter accumulation, days to maturity, number of pods per plant, number of grains per pod, test weight, grain yield, biological yield and harvest index. Economics of crop was also calculated to find out the economic feasibility for the farmers. 

Result: Result revealed that the significantly taller plants along with higher dry matter accumulation was observed under clusterbean variety Bundel Guar-2 (BG-2). Clusterbean variety Gujarat Guar-2 (GG-2) taken least number of days to maturity, however, highest number of days to maturity was taken by RGC-986 and BG-1. Significantly higher number of pods per plant was observed under RGC-1033. HG-365 resulted into significantly higher number of grains per pod and BG-1 recorded significantly higher test weight. RGC-1033 proved significantly better in terms of grain yield, harvest index and net returns. In terms of stover and biological yield BG-2 proved significantly superior.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces JX-Graph 1.0, a conceptual framework that integrates graph-theoretic and information-theoretic metrics-network tension (Φ), symmetry divergence (∆ sym), jump-history entropy (JHET), and description-length change (∆ MDL)-to detect and characterize interventions in digital platforms. Unlike previous approaches that attempted to equate compression efficiency with complexity-based evaluation, we explicitly avoid normative judgments. Instead, we frame interventions as deviations from a statistical baseline, quantified through measurable changes in complexity. To illustrate feasibility, we apply the framework first to a minimal toy model (cycle graph C 6), and then extend to a stochastic block model, demonstrating how localized interventions propagate detectable shifts across the proposed metrics. Our primary contribution lies in the unified integration of these metrics into a diagnostic dashboard for exploratory analysis. We openly acknowledge the conceptual and preliminary nature of this work: scalability to real-world, large-scale platforms remains unresolved; the definition of appropriate baselines and thresholds is nontrivial; and the interpretation of complexity shifts requires contextual judgment by human auditors and regulators. JX-Graph 1.0 should therefore be understood as a proof-of-concept, outlining a potential pathway toward more transparent, quantitative tools for platform governance.

title: Africa and the Complexity of Credit: Information, Meaning, and the Measure of Trust

detail.title: Africa and the Complexity of Credit: Information, Meaning, and the Measure of Trust
detail.abstract: This paper reinterprets credit rating as an act of casting complexity. It views each rating not as a neutral indicator but as a condensation of belief-a cognitive compression of the dynamic interplay among state, market, and society. Within Africa's political economy, credit thus becomes a mirror of adaptation rather than a measure of solvency. The paper positions Africa's credit narrative inside the broader evolution of global finance, showing how the practice of rating grew from mercantile observation into a planetary language of legitimacy. It traces how this language, once devised for industrial markets, extended into Africa through the mechanisms of structural adjustment, liberalisation, and Eurobond issuance. These processes turned credit rating into a tool of governance and embedded Africa within a global feedback loop of expectation and perception. Against this backdrop, the African Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) is presented not merely as an institution but as a reflexive operator-a continental learning mechanism that transforms Africa from an object of measurement into a subject of knowledge.

detail.title: Algorithmic Influence on Political Awareness and Narratives: How Instagram's Engagement System Influences the Civic Understanding of the Indian Youth
detail.abstract:
This study investigates how Instagram’s engagement-maximizing algorithm systematically influences the civic understanding of Indian youth by creating an algorithmic penalty for political content. While platforms are crucial for youth political awareness, their attention-economy design is hypothesized to inadvertently suppress civic discourse in favor of high-fluency entertainment.

A quantitative analysis of 220 content posts across Political and Entertainment categories was conducted. The methodology involved Natural Language Processing (NLP) to extract linguistic features (readability, sentiment), a Mann-Whitney U test for median comparison, and Negative Binomial Regression to model engagement as a function of content features. Content category was validated using Logistic Regression with TF-IDF features (Accuracy: 86%).

Findings confirmed a significant and severe disparity: Entertainment posts received over 27 times the median engagement of Political posts (p < 0.001, Cliff’s Delta = -0.675). Regression analysis revealed the categorical variable is_political to be the single strongest negative predictor (coef = -2.8718, p < 0.001), corresponding to a 94% reduction in expected engagement, independent of sentiment or complexity. This categorical penalty, driven by topic-specific keywords, indicates a structural bias.

The results demonstrate that algorithmic design on Instagram prioritizes low-effort entertainment over civic relevance. This mechanism fundamentally limits the exposure of young users to critical political information, posing risks to democratic literacy and establishing a definitive barrier within the algorithmic public sphere.

detail.abstract: The document presents recommendations for sustainable accommodation centers in Romania, focusing on long-term housing solutions for Ukrainian refugees. Developed through a joint effort by UNHCR, the Department for Emergency Situations (Ministry of Interior, Romania), and the Centre for the Comparative Study on Migration, it assesses five collective centers across the country. The report highlights key challenges such as insecure funding, infrastructure deficiencies, and limited access to essential services. It provides strategic recommendations to enhance sustainability, improve living conditions, and ensure preparedness for future emergencies. Additionally, it underscores the role of collective centers in supporting both refugees and vulnerable local populations.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Begum, Shamshad & Sreevidhya, S & Feroz, S & Mr, Begum & Aravind, & Prabu, S Raja. (2025). AN ANALYSIS ON ENGLISH NOVELS AND STORIES Title: An Analysis on English Novels and Stories.

detail.abstract: Beginning in the late 19th century and continuing up to the present day, this chapter follows the development of the English novel and short story. It argues that the contemporary age is characterised by a severe departure from the realism of the Victorian era and a persistent examination of the relationship between subjective awareness and narrative structure. It starts with a look at the works of early modernists like Thomas Hardy and Henry James, who shattered the secure, morally regulated world of their contemporaries with their introduction of psychological complexity and narrative ambiguity. Next, the chapter explores the groundbreaking methods of High Modernism (about 1918–1939), with an emphasis on the growth of stream of consciousness by writers such as James Joyce and Virginia Woolf, who aimed to portray the disjointed and inchoate character of the inner life during a world still recovering from the Great War's trauma. After this, the focus shifts to the postwar era, when postmodernism first began to take shape (about 1945–1980). Here we look at how Samuel Beckett and John Fowles, two of Modernism's most playful and skeptical followers, used techniques like pastiche, irony, and metafiction to cast doubt on the veracity of big tales and objective reality. Finally, the chapter assesses the contemporary literary landscape (c. 1980-present), highlighting its defining characteristic of pluralism.
